title: The class number one theorem without Heegner, kernel-checked twice in Lean 4: d <= 652 from the 7/8 quasi-Riemann hypothesis, and a determinant proof with no L-functions
description:
Lean 4 formalizations, certificate generators, numerical checks and two papers proving the class number one theorem for imaginary quadratic fields without Heegner's method: for squarefree m ≥ 1, Q(√−m) has class number one if and only if m ∈ {1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163}. The repository contains two independent proofs of the same Lean statement, with the same trust base. Written for T. Tao's tenth-discriminant AI-math challenge of 20 October 2026. Version 1.1.0 adds the second proof (directory determinant/) and its paper; the first proof, its certificates and its paper are unchanged from version 1.0.1.

First proof (the 7/8 route). Under class number one, the Dedekind zeta function is half an Epstein zeta function and equals ζ(s)L(s,χ). The Chowla–Selberg formula, with an explicit remainder proved in Lean, continues it to s = 7/8. OpenAI's zero-free region Re s > 7/8 for Dirichlet L-functions (openai/math, family 003, commit adc7f124) gives L(7/8,χ) ≥ 0 while ζ(7/8) < 0, forcing d ≤ 652, proved in Lean about Mathlib's riemannZeta and Gamma. Kernel-checked split-prime witnesses dispose of the 190 remaining fields, and the Minkowski bound proves the converse for the nine. The route was worked out in the comments of Tao's post.

Second proof (the determinant route). No L-function, no zeta function and no zero-free theorem is in its closure, and it needs only Mathlib. Under class number one with q = |disc K| ≥ 2^15, every prime below q/4 is inert and every split prime is a value of the norm form; a lattice count makes split primes sparse and yields an inert prime R in (q^4, q^5]. Green's derivative determinant on a grid of algebraic integers is nonzero modulo R by van Dijk's finite-field argument, Frobenius makes it divisible by a large power of every inert prime p ≤ R, and its complex size is too small for that. Below 2^15, a residue sieve over 4,095 integers, checked by the kernel, and two lemmas at p = 2 leave only the nine fields. The argument is that of the companion note twinheterodox/tenth-discriminant, companions/elementary, commit 64694aae, building on contributions of L. Silberman, K. Pratt, B. Green and R. van Dijk; the credits are in the README and the paper. The closure still contains integration, the Minkowski convex-body theorem and Mathlib's Gamma function, so the proof is not called elementary.

Verification. The statement uses only Mathlib definitions. Each proof depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Comparator (leanprover/comparator v4.34.0) accepts each under two independent kernels, nanoda and Lean's, and rejects tampered statements; the runs were local and not sandboxed. For the first proof, OpenAI's Lean proof of the 7/8 theorem is inside the checked dependency closure, not an assumption, and an independent replay by a separate AI review session (its own build of the project's modules and of nanoda, against the same verified dependency tree, with the same Comparator and lean4export binaries, on the same machine; local, not sandboxed) accepted the proof under both kernels, rejected two further tampers, and its closure audit agrees with ours. A clean copy of the formalization directory builds from the published instructions. For the determinant route, a closure audit of 69,295 constants found only the three standard axioms and no constant from Mathlib's L-series, Euler-product, zeta or modular-form modules or from outside Mathlib. An independent replay by a separate AI review session (its own build of the project's modules and of nanoda, with the same Comparator and lean4export binaries, on the same machine; local, not sandboxed) accepted the theorem under both kernels, its closure audit agrees, and five further controls of its own were rejected.

Status. Not refereed. OpenAI's manuscript and the companion note are unrefereed, although the Lean proofs are kernel-checked. The work was produced with extensive AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), with independent AI review; see the README.
